title: Silicon Valley races to train robots, starting with laundry-folding
excerpt: Sunday Robotics, Weave, and 1X are all starting with the same core task: laundry. Here's why it has become their favorite gateway into the home.
content_html:
Before Silicon Valley's robots take over, they have to learn to fold your underwear.

In recent months, some of the buzziest robotics startups — including Figure AI, Sunday Robotics, and Weave Robotics — have shown off robots that autonomously fold clothes. Together, the companies have raised billions of dollars at lofty valuations, as investors bet that home robots are finally nearing a commercial breakthrough.

We were promised robot butlers. For now, Silicon Valley would like to help you match your socks.

Home robotics companies are focusing on laundry because it's an ideal first task. It is difficult enough to showcase a machine's intelligence and physical control, and safe enough that failure carries few consequences, roboticists say. It is also a chore almost everyone does, and few enjoy. Consumers don't need to know how AI works to appreciate a robot that turns a crumpled pile of clothes into a neat stack.

Teaching a robot to fold clothing has long been a "holy grail" of the field, said roboticist and Spelman College president Ayanna Howard. That's because robots must learn to handle "deformable objects" — clothes that bunch, fold, and wrinkle — and manipulate them with enough precision to fold them well.

"This is one of the most challenging dexterous manipulation tasks for a humanoid robot," Figure wrote in a blog post last year. Sunday CEO Tony Zhao told Business Insider that the company chose laundry partly because it "looks for hard things to do."

Yet when a robot fails, the stakes are low.

"If you drop a piece of clothing, it's not going to break," Howard said.

The robotics industry has been through laundry hype cycles before. The Japanese company behind the $16,000 laundry-folding robot, Laundroid, filed for bankruptcy in 2019, and FoldiMate made repeated splashes at the Consumer Electronics Show in the late 2010s but never shipped a product.

High costs and poor reliability undid those earlier efforts. Today's startups say that advances in AI, cheaper hardware, and a flood of talent and capital into physical AI will make this generation different — and capable of doing far more than laundry.

"For the longest time, the technology just wasn't there," Weave Robotics CEO Kaan Dogrusoz told Business Insider. "But then, everything changed."

Whether that’s true is about to be tested outside the lab. The latest robots are expensive, and their reliability in real homes remains unknown because few have been deployed. While this generation can fold laundry much faster than its predecessors, a single item can still take minutes to fold, and unfamiliar clothing can leave the machines stumped.

Sunday plans to place its robot in homes through a beta program this fall. Weave and 1X expect to begin delivering robots to customers later this year.

Why laundry is a gateway into the home

Robotics companies are starting with laundry because it's a bounded task inside the home, a tough environment for robots to navigate.

"The home is the ultimate unstructured environment," said Matei Ciocarlie, a mechanical engineering professor at Columbia University who works on robotics.

Most robots operate in controlled environments such as factories and warehouses, where their surroundings and movements can be tightly defined. They are often separated from people for safety.

The home, by comparison, is a hellscape for robots. Every room is an obstacle course. Pets dart underfoot, and toddlers crawl across the floor, threatening to send machines into a faceplant.

When folding laundry, a robot can stay in one corner while a hamper of clothes is brought to it, rather than having to navigate the entire house. Dogrusoz cited this as the reason Weave chose laundry as the first task.

"It's an attempt to put bounds on the craziness," Ciocarlie said.

What comes after laundry?

Teaching a robot to fold laundry is one thing. Convincing people to pay thousands of dollars for it is another.

Weave's Isaac, for instance, costs $8,000 upfront, or $449 a month through a subscription. For most households, it would likely be cheaper to outsource the chore to a laundromat or a person. Or, as Howard put it: "That's what kids are for."

For these robots to make economic sense, they need to do far more than fold clothes.

Sunday's AI system, for instance, is learning chores including vacuuming, organizing toys, fastening zippers, and making coffee. 1X is marketing its humanoid robot NEO as a personal housekeeper capable of folding laundry, organizing shelves, and tidying rooms. Weave declined to say which task it is tackling next.

Howard said consumers are unlikely to seriously consider buying a home robot until it can perform enough useful tasks to justify its price, like heating dinner before its owner gets home, mowing the lawn, or cleaning the pool. The challenge will be building a single robot that can do all of these things.

Jason Corso, a robotics professor at the University of Michigan, said companies are "stuck in an appliance mindset," building robots around individual chores rather than machines that can understand context and adapt to people's needs.

For many of these companies, getting robots into homes to fold laundry is also the start of what they hope will become an expanding data flywheel. Robotics startups are scrambling for real-world data needed to train the "brains" of their machines. While large language models are trained on internet data, there is no comparable dataset for the physical world. Sunday, for example, trains its AI models on people doing everyday tasks in $200 sensor-equipped gloves that mirror its robots' hands.

The most valuable data — the kind that could help companies truly master laundry and expand into other tasks — may come from the robots themselves as they encounter the countless edge cases of real homes.

A truly general-purpose home robot — the robot butler Silicon Valley has long promised — is still many years away, Corso said.

blocks.html_en: For many of these companies, getting robots into homes to fold laundry is also the start of what they hope will become an expanding data flywheel. Robotics startups are scrambling for real-world data needed to train the "brains" of their machines. While large language models are trained on internet data, there is no comparable dataset for the physical world. Sunday, for example, trains its AI models on people doing everyday tasks in $200 sensor-equipped gloves that mirror its robots' hands.

content_html_zh:
在硅谷的机器人接管之前，它们必须学会折叠内衣。

近几个月来，一些最热门的机器人初创公司——包括Figure AI、Sunday Robotics和Weave Robotics——都展示了自动折叠衣服的机器人。 随着投资者押注家用机器人终于接近商业突破，这些公司已经以极高的估值筹集了数十亿美元。

他们向我们承诺会有机器人管家。 现在，硅谷愿意帮助你搭配袜子。

家庭机器人公司专注于洗衣，因为这是理想的首要任务。 机器人专家表示，展示机器的智能和物理控制非常困难，而且足够安全，即使出现故障也不会造成什么后果。 这也是几乎每个人都会做的苦差事，但很少有人喜欢。 消费者不需要知道人工智能是如何工作的，就能欣赏机器人将一堆皱巴巴的衣服变成整齐的一摞的机器人。

机器人学家兼斯佩尔曼学院院长艾安娜·霍华德表示，教机器人折叠衣服长期以来一直是该领域的“圣杯”。 这是因为机器人必须学会处理“可变形的物体”——会起皱、折叠和起皱的衣服——并以足够的精度操纵它们以很好地折叠它们。

“对于人形机器人来说，这是最具挑战性的灵巧操作任务之一，”图去年在一篇博客文章中写道。 《Sunday》首席执行官托尼·赵告诉《商业内幕》，该公司选择洗衣业务的部分原因是它“寻找困难的事情做”。

然而，当机器人出现故障时，风险就很低。

“即使你掉了一件衣服，它也不会破裂，”霍华德说。

机器人行业之前就经历过洗衣炒作周期。 售价 16,000 美元的洗衣折叠机器人背后的日本公司 Laundroid 于 2019 年申请破产，而 FoldiMate 在 2010 年代末的消费电子展上屡屡引起轰动，但从未发货。

高成本和差的可靠性使早期的努力付诸东流。 如今的初创公司表示，人工智能的进步、更便宜的硬件以及大量人才和资本投入物理人工智能将使这一代人与众不同，并且能够做的不仅仅是洗衣服。

Weave Robotics 首席执行官 Kaan Dogrusoz 告诉《商业内幕》：“很长一段时间以来，这项技术都不存在。” “但是后来，一切都变了。”

这是否属实将在实验室外进行测试。 最新的机器人价格昂贵，而且它们在真实家庭中的可靠性仍然未知，因为很少有人部署。 虽然这一代产品折叠衣物的速度比前代产品快得多，但折叠一件物品仍然需要几分钟的时间，而且不熟悉的衣服可能会让机器陷入困境。

Sunday 计划今年秋天通过测试计划将其机器人放置在家里。 Weave 和 1X 预计将于今年晚些时候开始向客户提供机器人。

为什么洗衣房是进入家庭的门户

机器人公司从洗衣开始，因为这是一项在家里进行的有限任务，对于机器人来说是一个艰难的环境。

“家是最终的非结构化环境，”哥伦比亚大学机械工程教授马泰·乔卡利（Matei Ciocarlie）说，他从事机器人技术研究。

大多数机器人在工厂和仓库等受控环境中运行，它们的周围环境和运动可以被严格定义。 为了安全起见，他们经常与人分开。

相比之下，家庭对于机器人来说就是地狱。 每个房间都是障碍训练场。 宠物在脚下飞奔，幼儿在地板上爬行，威胁要将机器送入工厂。

折叠衣物时，机器人可以待在一个角落，同时将一篮子衣服送到它那里，而不必在整个房子里走来走去。 Dogrusoz 将此作为 Weave 选择洗衣作为首要任务的原因。

“这是一种限制疯狂行为的尝试，”乔卡莉说。

洗完衣服之后会发生什么？

教机器人叠衣服是一回事。 说服人们为此支付数千美元是另一回事。

例如，Weave 的 Isaac 预付费用为 8,000 美元，订阅后每月费用为 449 美元。 对于大多数家庭来说，将家务外包给自助洗衣店或个人可能会更便宜。 或者，正如霍华德所说：“这就是孩子的意义。”

为了使这些机器人具有经济意义，它们需要做的不仅仅是折叠衣服。

例如，周日的人工智能系统正在学习家务活，包括吸尘、整理玩具、拉紧拉链和煮咖啡。 1X 正在将其人形机器人 NEO 定位为私人管家，能够叠衣服、整理架子和整理房间。 Weave 拒绝透露下一步要处理哪项任务。

霍华德表示，消费者不太可能认真考虑购买家用机器人，除非它能够执行足够多的有用任务以证明其价格合理，例如在主人回家之前加热晚餐、修剪草坪或清洁游泳池。 挑战将是建造一个可以完成所有这些事情的机器人。

密歇根大学机器人学教授杰森·科索表示，企业“陷入了一种设备思维”，围绕个人琐事构建机器人，而不是能够理解环境并适应人们需求的机器。

对于许多这样的公司来说，让机器人进入家庭折叠衣物也是他们希望成为不断扩大的数据飞轮的开始。 机器人初创公司正在争夺训练机器“大脑”所需的真实数据。 虽然大型语言模型是根据互联网数据进行训练的，但物理世界没有可比的数据集。 例如，Sunday 训练其人工智能模型，让人们戴着价值 200 美元、配备传感器的手套（模仿其机器人的手）执行日常任务。

最有价值的数据——能够帮助公司真正掌握洗衣并扩展到其他任务的数据——可能来自机器人本身，因为它们遇到了真实家庭中无数的边缘情况。

科尔索说，真正的通用家庭机器人——硅谷长期以来承诺的机器人管家——距离实现还需要很多年。
